scenarios.title: Everyone Starts at Chapter 1
scenarios.situation: A course forces all learners through Chapter 1 regardless of background. Experienced learners disengage from boredom; true beginners are lost by Chapter 3 because gaps were never detected.
scenarios.prompt: What fixes both problems at once?
evidence:
experienced learners: 70% drop by week 2
beginners: 55% fail the midterm
choices: Adaptive placement that maps each learner's prior knowledge and starts them at their own frontier
Keep the linear path but make Chapter 1 skippable on request
Let learners self-place with no assessment
Remove placement entirely - motivation matters more than starting point
scenarios.why: Placement against a knowledge structure puts each learner at their own learnable frontier: experienced learners skip mastered material, beginners get routed to missing prerequisites. Self-placement is unreliable (Dunning-Kruger cuts both ways), and a skippable Chapter 1 still never diagnoses the beginners' gaps.
scenarios.hint: What single mechanism serves the bored expert and the lost beginner simultaneously?

scenarios.title: The All-Nighter
scenarios.situation: A learner has a knowledge check in 7 days. Her plan: re-read the textbook chapter three times the night before. Her last three checks show the same pattern - decent immediately after cramming, failed reassessment two weeks later.
scenarios.prompt: What study plan actually builds durable mastery?
choices: Spaced retrieval practice: short self-testing sessions spread across the 7 days, with reassessment of weak items
Re-read the chapter three times the night before, more carefully this time
Highlight the textbook thoroughly - active marking aids memory
Pull one all-nighter instead of spreading effort - focus beats spacing
scenarios.why: Retrieval practice (testing yourself) strengthens memory far more than re-reading, and spacing the sessions exploits the spacing effect - her own history shows cramming produces fragile, short-lived performance. Highlighting feels productive but barely beats doing nothing.
scenarios.hint: Her history is an experiment with three trials. What did the cramming condition actually produce?

scenarios.title: Failing Percents
scenarios.situation: A learner has failed the 'percents' topic four times. Each failure triggers more percent worksheets, each failed the same way. Her knowledge check shows decimals at 40% and fractions at 55%.
scenarios.prompt: What should the system do next?
evidence: 4 failed attempts at percents; more percent worksheets assigned each time
choices: Route her back to remediate decimals and fractions - percents depend on them
Assign more percent worksheets at higher difficulty
Lower the passing threshold for percents so she can move on
Skip percents and move to the next topic
scenarios.why: Percents sit downstream of decimals and fractions in the prerequisite structure; drilling a downstream topic while its prerequisites are unmastered is futile - the evidence shows the foundation is the gap. Remediating prerequisites is exactly what a knowledge-space model prescribes; lowering the bar or skipping just relocates the failure.
scenarios.hint: Can someone master percents while decimals sit at 40%? Where in the prerequisite chain is the real gap?

scenarios.title: The 50-Question Placement
scenarios.situation: Placement takes every learner through the same fixed 50-question test. Strong learners answer 40 questions far below their level; weak learners suffer through 40 questions far above theirs. Completion rates are falling.
evidence: 'too easy and boring' / 'too hard and humiliating'
choices: Computerized adaptive testing: each response updates the ability estimate and the next item targets that level
Cut the fixed test to 20 random questions
Make the 50 questions untimed to reduce stress
Grade the fixed test on a curve instead
scenarios.why: IRT-based adaptive testing converges on the learner's ability in far fewer items because every question is informative - no floor or ceiling effects, no wasted items. Fewer random questions just add noise; untimed does not fix mis-targeted items; curving re-labels the same bad measurement.
scenarios.hint: What information does a question far above or below your level actually provide? How would you pick the next question?

scenarios.title: Memorizing the Item Bank
scenarios.situation: Learners discover the placement test draws from a small fixed item bank. Scores rise, but proctored reassessments show no real learning - students memorized the specific items and their answers.
evidence: unproctored placement: 85% avg | proctored reassessment: 52% avg
60 fixed items, widely shared among learners
choices: Large calibrated item pools with prerequisite-gated progression - memorizing items cannot fake the underlying knowledge state
Add more items of the same style to the fixed bank
Proctor every assessment heavily
Ignore it - high scores are the goal
scenarios.why: A large pool makes memorizing every item impractical, and prerequisite gating means progress requires the actual knowledge structure, not item recall - the reassessment gap closes because there is nothing to game. More same-style items just expand the cheat sheet; universal proctoring is expensive and treats the symptom.
scenarios.hint: What exactly did the learners memorize - knowledge, or items? Which design makes that distinction irrelevant?

scenarios.title: Where to Set the Bar
scenarios.situation: A course team debates the mastery threshold for advancing: 50% ('don't block learners'), 100% on a single attempt ('true mastery'), or something in between. Dropout and downstream-failure data are on the table.
evidence:
50% threshold -> 60% fail the next module
100% single-attempt -> 45% dropout at the gate
choices: A high bar (around 80-90%) with a reassessment and remediation path - mastery learning's classic compromise
50% - keeping learners moving matters most
100% on a single attempt - anything less is not mastery
No threshold - let learners decide when they are ready
scenarios.why: Bloom's mastery learning sets the bar high (80-90%) but makes time the variable: learners who miss it get diagnosis and retakes instead of permanent failure. The evidence shows 50% passes learners who then fail downstream, while single-attempt 100% converts a learning gate into a dropout machine.
scenarios.hint: What do the two failure modes in the evidence have in common - and what policy avoids both?

lessons.title: Adaptive Learning Foundations - Core concepts
concepts: Mastery learning (Bloom): advancement depends on reaching roughly 80-90% mastery, not on the calendar. Time becomes the variable; learning is the constant.

Knowledge Space Theory (Doignon and Falmagne) formalizes prerequisites: a learner's knowledge state is the set of mastered items, and only items whose prerequisites are all mastered sit on the learnable 'fringe'. Adaptive systems assess by navigating this structure.
Vygotsky's Zone of Proximal Development: target tasks just beyond what the learner can do alone, with scaffolding that fades. Too easy bores; too hard frustrates - adaptivity lives in the gap.
Item Response Theory powers computerized adaptive testing: each response updates the ability estimate, and the next item is chosen at that level - converging in far fewer questions than a fixed form.
Retrieval practice and spacing beat re-reading and cramming: testing strengthens memory, and spaced intervals exploit the spacing effect. Schedule reassessments, not just lessons.
Close the loop fast: assess, diagnose the missing prerequisite, remediate, reassess. The unit of adaptation is the knowledge state, not the test score.

example.code:
prereq = {"fractions": set(),
          "decimals": {"fractions"},
          "percents": {"decimals", "fractions"}}
mastered = {"fractions", "decimals"}
fringe = [item for item, ps in prereq.items()
          if item not in mastered and ps <= mastered]
print("learnable next:", fringe)
example.walkthrough: The fringe is every unmastered item whose prerequisites are all mastered - here, percents. An adaptive system offers exactly this set next, never items the learner is not ready for and never ones already known.

pitfalls: Common trap: optimizing the test score instead of the knowledge state - scores can be gamed; prerequisite structure cannot.
Common trap: one fixed curriculum for everyone - prior-knowledge variance makes linear paths wasteful for half the class.
Common trap: placing once and never reassessing - knowledge states shift; forgetting is real and measurable.
Common trap: reading engagement dashboards as learning - clicks and time-on-page do not equal mastery.
lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab.

labs.title: Compute the Learnable Fringe
labs.objective: Implement a prerequisite graph and compute the fringe - the set of items a learner is ready to learn next.
steps: Write fringe.py with a prereq dict for 6 topics (fractions, decimals, percents, ratios, algebra, geometry) and their prerequisite sets.
Implement fringe(mastered): return items not mastered whose prerequisites are all mastered.
Test with mastered = {'fractions'} and print the fringe.
Test with mastered = {'fractions', 'decimals', 'percents'} and confirm the fringe advances correctly.
Add a topic with two prerequisites and verify it appears only when both are mastered.

checks.hint: Print the fringe for each test knowledge state - the script output must include the word 'fringe'.

labs.title: Simulate Adaptive Testing
labs.objective: Simulate a tiny adaptive test that steps difficulty up on correct answers and down on wrong ones, then compare its length to a fixed form.
steps: Write cat.py: model a learner with true ability 0.6 and items with difficulty 0.0-1.0.
Start at difficulty 0.5; after each response move the estimate up or down by a shrinking step.
Simulate 10 items, printing the estimate after each response.
Print the final ability estimate and its error vs the true 0.6.
In a comment, note how many fixed-form items you would need for similar precision.

checks.hint: The simulation must print the evolving ability estimate - output should include the word 'ability'.

simulations.title: The learner stuck below mastery
simulations.brief: A learner has attempted the subnetting module 5 times, scoring 55–62% against an 80% mastery bar. The system keeps serving the same difficulty. Diagnose why the loop is not adapting.

steps.symptom: 5 attempts, scores flat at ~60%, same item difficulty each time, no hint usage, no prerequisite review assigned.
options: The learner is not trying hard enough — assign more attempts

The adaptation is broken: flat scores at 60% signal the items are outside the learner's zone of proximal development — the system should drop difficulty, diagnose the misconception, or route to prerequisites instead of repeating
Lower the mastery bar to 60%
The content is fine — some learners just fail
evidence: Attempts 1–5: 58, 61, 55, 62, 59. Item difficulty: constant 0.72. Hint requests: 0. Prerequisite 'binary arithmetic' status: not attempted.

Zone of proximal development: learning happens just beyond current ability with support. Flat scores far below mastery indicate items too hard, a misconception, or missing prerequisites — never 'try the same thing again.'
steps.explain: Mastery learning requires the system to respond to evidence. Five flat attempts are five measurements saying 'this is not working' — the correct response is easier items, targeted hints, or prerequisite routing, not repetition.

steps.symptom: Diagnosis: missing prerequisite (binary arithmetic never attempted). What should the system have done at attempt 2?
options: Kept serving subnetting items — persistence builds character
Detected the flat pattern, administered a prerequisite probe, and routed to binary arithmetic remediation before returning to subnetting
Skipped the learner ahead to the next module
Reset the attempt counter
evidence: Knowledge space theory: subnetting depends on binary arithmetic. A learner missing the prerequisite cannot master the dependent skill — the graph predicts the failure before it happens.
steps.explain: Knowledge space theory turns 'stuck' into a diagnosable state: trace the prerequisite graph, find the missing node, remediate it. The system should have known at attempt 2 what the graph already said.

simulations.debrief: Adaptive systems earn the name by adapting: flat scores are a signal, prerequisites are a graph, and 'try again' is not a pedagogy. Diagnose the cause, route to the missing foundation, then return.

simulations.title: Choose the next item: the adaptive engine's decision
simulations.brief: The engine estimates a learner's subnetting ability at 65% (±10%). Three candidate items: easy (95% expected success), medium (70%), hard (35%). Choose the next item.

steps.symptom: Ability estimate 65% ±10%. Candidates: easy (95% success), medium (70%), hard (35%). Goal: maximum information about the learner's true ability plus productive struggle.
options: The easy item — success builds confidence
The medium item — ~70% success probability sits in the zone of proximal development and maximally reduces uncertainty about the ability estimate
The hard item — challenge reveals the ceiling
Random — the engine should not play favorites
evidence: Item response theory: information is maximized when item difficulty matches learner ability. A 70%-success item both teaches (productive struggle) and measures (tightens the estimate).
95% items teach nothing and measure nothing; 35% items frustrate and also measure poorly (failure is uninformative about how far below).
steps.explain: Adaptive testing is measurement and teaching at once. The medium item is the only choice that does both: hard enough to inform, easy enough to learn from. Extremes waste the learner's time.

steps.symptom: The learner answers the medium item correctly but slowly (4x median time). How should the engine update its model?
options: Raise the ability estimate — correct is correct
Raise the estimate modestly but flag low fluency: correctness without fluency means the knowledge is fragile — schedule retrieval practice rather than advancing difficulty
Lower the estimate — slow means guessing
Ignore response time entirely
evidence: Mastery = accuracy + fluency. Slow-correct responses predict poor retention and transfer. The engine should bank the correctness but treat fluency as a separate skill dimension needing practice.
steps.explain: A correct answer is not the whole story. Fluency — speed plus accuracy — is what survives the forgetting curve. The engine's job is to notice the fragility and prescribe practice, not just advance the difficulty.

simulations.debrief: Every item selection is a bet: maximize information, keep the learner in productive struggle, and read the full response — correctness, time, and hints — before updating the model.

simulations.title: The impossible score jump
simulations.brief: A learner's ability estimate jumped from 40% to 95% in one 20-minute session, with median response time of 3 seconds per item. The integrity monitor flagged it. Respond.

steps.symptom: Session: 30 items, 29 correct, 3s median response time (cohort median: 48s). Previous 6 sessions: 35–45% ability, 50s+ responses.
options: Celebrate — the learner had a breakthrough

Treat as a probable integrity violation: the response pattern (impossible speed + discontinuous jump) indicates answer sharing or automation — invalidate the session and investigate before the estimate poisons downstream adaptation
Average it into the estimate
Ban the learner immediately
evidence: Flags: response time <10th percentile on 29/30 items; ability discontinuity >4 standard deviations; IP geolocation changed mid-session. Pattern matches answer-key use, not learning (learning curves are gradual).
Anomalous sessions are quarantined from the ability estimate pending review. Accusation requires evidence; invalidation requires only the anomaly.
steps.explain: Learning is gradual; cheating is discontinuous. The pattern — not the score — is the evidence. Quarantine the session so it cannot corrupt the adaptive model, then investigate fairly.

steps.symptom: Investigation: the learner's older sibling completed the session. The learner cooperated fully. Disposition?
options: Permanent ban — zero tolerance

Invalidate the session, reset the estimate to the pre-anomaly value, require a proctored re-assessment for the affected module, and record the integrity lesson — proportionate, restorative, and protective of the model's integrity
Count the 95% — the sibling is basically a tutor
Do nothing
evidence: Goal: protect measurement integrity while keeping the learner in the program. Proctored re-assessment re-establishes a trustworthy estimate; the record deters repetition.
steps.explain: The measurement must be protected (invalidate, re-assess) and the learner kept (restorative, not destructive). Integrity systems that only punish teach evasion; systems that re-measure teach honesty.

simulations.debrief: Adaptive systems are measurement instruments — contaminated data corrupts every downstream decision. Quarantine anomalies fast, investigate fairly, re-measure cleanly.

simulations.title: Schedule the retrieval practice
simulations.brief: A learner mastered subnetting (92%, fluent) 7 days ago. The forgetting curve predicts 60% retention today. Decide the retrieval-practice schedule.

steps.symptom: Mastered 7 days ago at 92% fluent. Predicted retention today: 60%. Exam in 30 days. Options: re-study the chapter, one retrieval session today, or spaced retrieval sessions.
options: Re-study the chapter — re-reading feels productive
Spaced retrieval: a low-stakes recall session today, then expanding intervals (3 days, 7 days, 14 days) — retrieval practice beats re-study for durable retention
One big cram session the night before the exam
Nothing — 92% was mastery
evidence: Testing effect: retrieval practice produces ~50% better long-term retention than re-study. Expanding intervals match the forgetting curve — practice arrives just as the memory fades.
Without practice: 92% -> 60% (7d) -> 35% (30d). With spaced retrieval: 92% -> 85%+ at 30d.
steps.explain: Mastery is not permanent — it decays on a curve. Spaced retrieval re-strengthens the memory at the moment of fading, which is exactly when practice buys the most durability. Re-reading feels fluent because it is familiar, not because it is learned.

steps.symptom: The learner dreads the retrieval sessions ('tests are stressful'). How do you keep the schedule without the anxiety?
options: Drop the schedule — wellbeing first
Make retrieval low-stakes: no grades, immediate feedback, framed as practice — the learning benefit comes from the retrieval attempt, not the score
Make them high-stakes to motivate
Replace retrieval with videos
evidence: Low-stakes retrieval preserves the testing effect while removing the threat response. Feedback after the attempt (not during) maximizes learning.
steps.explain: The stress is in the stakes, not the retrieval. Keep the cognitive work (recall attempts) and remove the threat (grades, judgment) — the memory benefits stay, the anxiety goes.

simulations.debrief: Durable learning is scheduled forgetting-fighting: retrieval practice at expanding intervals, low stakes, with feedback. Design the schedule around the curve, not around the calendar.

simulations.title: Set the mastery threshold
simulations.brief: The course team debates the mastery bar: 70%, 80%, or 90%. Too low advances fragile learners; too high traps competent ones in remediation. Set the rule.

steps.symptom: Pilot data: at 70%, 22% of advancers fail the next module; at 90%, 31% of learners need 3+ remediation cycles and completion drops 18%. At 80%: 9% downstream failure, 12% need extended remediation.
options: 70% — keep completion high
80% with a fluency requirement — the pilot data minimizes total harm: downstream failures and remediation burden are both near their minimum
90% — standards matter most
No threshold — let learners self-assess
evidence: Total-harm curve is U-shaped: 70% harms downstream (fragile advancers), 90% harms here (trapped learners). 80% + fluency (accuracy at speed) is the observed minimum of combined harm.
Accuracy-only 80% still admits slow-correct fragility; adding a fluency bar (median time under threshold) cut downstream failure from 14% to 9% in the pilot.
steps.explain: Threshold-setting is harm minimization with data, not a values debate. The pilot measured both failure modes and found the minimum — and fluency separates real mastery from slow correct.

steps.symptom: Threshold set at 80% + fluency. One more decision: what happens to the learner at 79%?
options: Advance them — close enough
Targeted remediation on the specific failed subskills (not the whole module), then a focused re-assessment — the system knows exactly which items were missed
Restart the entire module
Hold them until they hit 80% on the full module retest
evidence: The 79% learner missed 3 of 4 items on one subskill (CIDR notation) and passed everything else. Whole-module repetition wastes 80% of their time.
steps.explain: The adaptive advantage is diagnosis: the system knows which subskill failed, so remediation targets exactly that. 'Close enough' advances fragility; whole-module repetition punishes precision with tedium.

simulations.debrief: Mastery thresholds are set by evidence, not tradition: measure both failure modes, pick the harm minimum, require fluency — and remediate the diagnosed gap, never the whole module.

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about the most technically difficult problem you have run into — a homelab, a broken environment, anything — and how you solved it.
points: Pick ONE problem with a real evidence trail: the symptom, what you measured, the hypothesis you tested
Show the loop: scope, observe, hypothesize, smallest safe change, validate — interviewers score the method, not just the fix
Name the tools (VM build, networking, logs) and the lesson it taught you
Close with the result in concrete terms: what works now that did not before
pitfalls: Choosing a story with no real obstacle (“I Googled it” is not a story)
Skipping validation — saying it worked without proving it
Rambling past two minutes without reaching the result

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you dealt with a frustrated customer or user while something was broken.
points: Lead with empathy and ownership: acknowledge the impact before the technical detail
Show translation: what you told them, in their language, plus the timeline you committed to
Show judgment: the narrow fix you chose and what you refused to do (e.g., disabling the control to clear the symptom)
Close with the relationship outcome, not just the technical one
pitfalls: Badmouthing the customer to sound decisive
Promising a timeline you could not keep
Framing the user as the problem rather than the situation

points: Connect prevention to something concrete: a moment you saw detection arrive too late, or a system you hardened
Tie their model to your instincts: deny-by-default matches how you already think about trust
Show service orientation: the Cyber Hero culture rewards the 2 a.m. helper — give an example of being one
Name one forward-looking reason: Zero Trust, the MSP mission, or the bootcamp community investment
pitfalls: Generic flattery with no specifics about the company
Leading with compensation, title, or location convenience
Claiming expertise in products you have only read about — frame it as studied, not mastered
Staying vague ('I analyzed the data') instead of naming what you connected.
Skipping your own role: what did YOU see that others missed?
No outcome: what changed because you joined the dots?
points: The scattered signals and why nobody had connected them yet
The specific links you drew between them (shared host, time, infrastructure)
What the bigger picture turned out to be and what action it drove
What the experience taught you about investigating
behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you connected scattered clues into a bigger picture that others had missed.

pitfalls: Claiming you fixed everything: credibility comes from trade-offs, not heroics.
Hiding the constraint: the limitation is what makes the prioritization story real.
No metric: 'better' needs a before-and-after.
points: The constraint (time, budget, staff) and the size of the backlog
How you decided what mattered most (what was reachable, what was critical)
What you did first and what you deliberately deferred
The measurable result of the prioritization
behavioral.prompt: Describe a time you had to prioritize risks or fixes with limited time or resources. How did you decide what came first?

pitfalls: Reciting jargon to a non-technical audience and calling it communication.
Skipping the audience's reaction: did they actually understand and act?
Making yourself the hero instead of the translator.
points: The technical finding and why it mattered
Who the audience was and what they cared about
How you reframed it (a picture, an analogy, a story)
What decision or action the audience took because they understood
behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you explained a complex technical finding to a non-technical audience and it changed a decision.
Tell me about a time you used automation or AI to solve a security problem.
points: The repetitive security task and what it cost in analyst time
The automation or AI approach you built and how you validated it
Measured outcome: time saved, detection gained, false positives changed
pitfalls: Describing the tool but never the validation
No measurable outcome

behavioral.prompt: Describe a time you had to decide whether to trust an automated security decision.
points: The stakes of the automated action and its blast radius
How you verified before acting (or the gate you built)
What happened and what you would automate differently next time
pitfalls: Saying you always trust the tool
No mention of blast radius or reversibility

Customers: 70,000+ organizations, sold heavily through the MSP channel

Interview address: 1901 Summit Tower Blvd, Orlando, FL 32810
Culture: in-office 5 days/week; free lunch; post-offer background + drug screening

sections.heading: Product stack
items: Allowlisting — default-deny execution control for apps, DLLs, scripts, installers
Ringfencing — constrains allowed apps: app-to-app, file, registry, network
Storage Control — USB/device policy by serial, user, file type, encryption
Elevation Control — just-in-time per-app admin, no standing rights
Network Control — host firewall; port/IP/dynamic-ACL rules; ZTNA foundation
Web Control — agent-based DNS/URL category filtering, works off-network
Cyber Hero MDR — 24/7/365 US-based response, ~60-second average
Testing Environment — one-button VDI sandbox; checks AV flags, canary files, registry changes

sections.heading: Rule strength (strongest to weakest)
items: Certificate/publisher rules — survive version updates
Hash rules — precise but break on every new version
Path rules — weakest; never in user-writable locations
Learning Mode catalogs before enforcement; Installation Mode pauses blocking — scope and time-box both

sections.heading: Terminal evidence commands
items: nmap <host> — which ports answer (22/80/443 open)
dig <name> — ANSWER SECTION with the A record
ss — listening sockets
systemctl status <svc> — unit state
journalctl -u <svc> — service logs
sha256sum <file> — real SHA-256 identity
grep <pattern> <file> — search the record
ps — what is actually running

sections.heading: Graph vocabulary
items: node — any entity tracked in the model (user, host, IP, domain, file hash, vulnerability)
edge — a labeled relationship between two nodes (logged into, resolved to, downloaded)
degree — number of edges on a node; high-degree nodes are attacker highways
centrality — how much traffic or how many paths flow through a node
directed edge — a relationship with a direction (A downloaded FROM B)
security graph — the living model of your whole environment as nodes and edges
attack graph — the subgraph of exploitable paths to your targets
knowledge graph — threat-intel indicators linked to campaigns and actors

sections.heading: Attack-graph playbook
items: inventory first — you cannot graph what you have not discovered
model flaws AND misconfigs as exploit edges
compute shortest paths to the crown jewels
find the choke point (highest betweenness on those paths)
break the path: patch, segment, or remove the edge
re-scan and re-run the graph to prove the path is gone
never trust yesterday's graph — redeployments redraw the map

sections.heading: Zero Trust + graphs
items: never trust, always verify — re-evaluate every access decision
assume breach — treat unexpected edges as hostile until proven otherwise
microsegmentation — allow-list approved edges, alert on new ones
ReBAC — policies are path queries on the identity graph
continuous verification — device/location/behavior edges change, trust follows
anomalous edge — a first-seen connection between strangers is the classic signal

sections.heading: ML detection vocabulary
items: Supervised learning — learns from labeled examples; strong on known threats, blind to novel ones
Unsupervised learning — finds structure without labels; clustering and dimensionality reduction
Anomaly detection — models 'normal' and flags deviations; the workhorse for novel threats
UEBA — user and entity behavior analytics: per-user baselines plus peer-group comparison
Feature engineering — encoding raw logs into model inputs (login velocity, rare processes, domain entropy)
Concept drift — model decay as attacker behavior and legitimate traffic shift over time

sections.heading: Detection metrics
items: Precision — of all flagged alerts, how many were real
Recall — of all real attacks, how many were flagged
Threshold tuning — sliding the decision cutoff trades precision against recall
Alert fatigue — when false positives train analysts to ignore the queue
DGA — domain generation algorithm; detected via character entropy of domain names

sections.heading: Agent and LLM security
items: Direct prompt injection — attacker input overrides app instructions (OWASP LLM01:2025, the #1 LLM risk)
Indirect prompt injection — hidden instructions inside retrieved data (email, web, docs)
Jailbreak — defeating the model's own safety policy; distinct from hijacking app behavior
Tool poisoning — malicious tool descriptions or metadata steer an agent to misuse its tools (MCP ecosystem risk)
Insecure output handling — executing or trusting model output without validation
Least-privilege tools — grant each tool only the scope its task requires

sections.heading: Adversarial ML and governance
items: Evasion — perturbing inputs at inference time to dodge a classifier
Poisoning — corrupting training data to corrupt the model
Extraction — querying a model to steal its behavior or parameters
MITRE ATLAS — knowledge base of adversarial ML tactics and techniques
Red-teaming and evals — adversarial testing of AI systems before deployment
Human-in-the-loop — required approval for high-impact or irreversible agent actions
SOAR — security orchestration, automation and response; automate enrichment, gate containment

glossary.def: Default-deny execution control: only explicitly approved applications, scripts, and installers may run.
Default-allow model: everything runs except recognized-bad items — the window zero-days live in.
Deny-by-default posture: unknown code, devices, or connections are refused unless explicitly approved.
Containment applied on top of allowlisting; restricts what a permitted app may do across app-to-app, file, registry, and network dimensions.
Agent mode that catalogs applications and dependencies and auto-builds policies before enforcement; temporarily disables file blocking.
Temporary mode that pauses file blocking for installs — must be tightly scoped and time-boxed.
Grants specific approved applications admin rights for standard users — just-in-time, per-app, time-boxed — without standing admin rights.
An elevated or trusted process spawning another tool (e.g., PowerShell) to inherit its privileges — countered by ringfencing the elevated process.
Device and path policy: USB approved by serial, user, file type, time, and encryption; unapproved devices do not connect.
Centrally managed host firewall; rules by port, source IP, and dynamic ACLs; egress allowlisting pins apps to approved destinations.
Zero Trust Network Access: per-session, per-application brokered connections (commonly over port 443) with no open inbound ports — deny-by-default for network access.
Portal queue where end-user software requests arrive for admin review and decision.
Real-time audit showing what was allowed or denied across endpoints — and why; the evidence layer for triage.
One-button cloud VDI sandbox launched from an approval request; logs AV flags, canary-file access, and registry/system changes.
24/7/365 US-based managed detection and response team; validates alerts, isolates hosts, acts on customer runbooks; ~60-second average response.
Design and operate as if the attacker already has a foothold — least privilege, containment, and monitoring everywhere.
Attacks that hijack trusted built-in tools (Word, PowerShell) instead of dropping malware — defeated by behavior containment, not signatures.
Scoped, ticketed, tested changes with validation and rollback — emergency speed never cancels the process.
A node in an attack graph representing a system or weakness, connected by edges that represent steps an attacker could take between them.
How central a node is to paths through the graph (for example, betweenness: how many shortest paths cross it).
The most valuable assets in the environment (customer data, finance systems, source code): what attack paths are measured against.
A labeled connection between two nodes, representing a relationship such as 'logged into' or 'resolved to'.
A graph of threat indicators (IPs, domains, hashes) linked to campaigns, actors, and each other through shared infrastructure.
The practice of mapping relationships in data to reveal hidden associations; rooted in Euler's 1736 graph theory, 1970s paper link charts, and post-2001 intelligence work.
A segment of the network so small that its allowed communications can be enumerated as a graph of approved edges.
An entity in the graph: a user, host, IP address, domain, file, or vulnerability.
Access control where policy is evaluated by traversing relationships on a graph (for example: user reports_to manager who owns the resource's project).
A machine-learning model that operates directly on graph structure to classify nodes or subgraphs, for example labeling attack vs normal behavior.
Monitoring user and entity behavior by modeling their normal relationship patterns and flagging structural anomalies.
ML trained on labeled examples; classifies new inputs into known categories.
ML approach that models normal behavior and flags statistically rare deviations.
Turning raw telemetry into numeric model inputs, e.g. login velocity or domain entropy.
Share of flagged alerts that were real; the false-positive economics of the queue.
Share of real attacks the detector flagged; the miss rate's complement.
Decay of model performance as the data distribution shifts over time.
Attacker-crafted instructions that override an LLM application's intended behavior; direct (user input) or indirect (retrieved data).
Crafted input that defeats an LLM's own safety policy or refusal behavior.
Malicious tool descriptions or metadata that manipulate an AI agent into misusing its tools.
Failing to validate LLM output before acting on it, e.g. executing generated commands.
Adversarial ML technique: perturbing inputs to cross a classifier's decision boundary.
Adversarial Threat Landscape for AI Systems; MITRE's knowledge base of AI attack tactics.
Security orchestration, automation and response; playbooks that enrich automatically and gate containment on humans.
Required human approval before high-impact or irreversible automated actions.

checklist: Sixty-second company brief rehearsed out loud: year, city, philosophy, three products, one milestone
Two STAR stories ready: hardest technical problem; a frustrated customer or user
“Why ThreatLocker / why cybersecurity” answer tied to prevention and service, not slogans
Ringfencing explained in one plain-English sentence (the Word-on-a-leash version)
Elevation Control answer ready: just-in-time, per-app, time-boxed, ringfenced, logged
Triage loop memorized: scope → observe → hypothesize → smallest safe change → validate → explain
Three questions to ask them: team on-call shape, approval SLA expectations, what “most helpful” looks like on the team
Logistics: 1901 Summit Tower Blvd, Orlando FL; in-office role; ID and references ready
Define your crown jewels before you model anything.
Build the asset-and-access graph from live sources (scans, configs, identity), not from the CMDB alone.
Model vulnerabilities AND misconfigurations as exploit edges.
Compute shortest attack paths to each crown jewel; name the choke points.
Prioritize remediation by path risk, not by raw severity score.
Express at least one access policy as a relationship path (ReBAC pilot).
Baseline approved communication edges per segment; alert on first-seen edges.
Brief the next incident or risk review with the graph, not a spreadsheet.
Can you explain supervised vs unsupervised vs anomaly detection with a security example for each?
Can you name three log features you would engineer for a C2 detector and why?
Can you walk through a UEBA alert (baseline, deviation, verification) end to end?
Can you explain the precision/recall tradeoff and how you would set a threshold for a fatigued SOC?
Can you define concept drift and describe a retraining process?
Can you distinguish direct vs indirect prompt injection and jailbreaking?
Can you explain tool poisoning in the MCP ecosystem and three controls against it?
Can you describe insecure output handling and how you would validate agent output?
Can you name the three adversarial ML attack classes and one defense for evasion?
Can you design a SOAR playbook gate: what automates freely, what needs human approval?

media.title: Allowlisting vs blocklisting: default-deny vs default-allow
media.caption: Default-deny stops unknown code without a signature; default-allow runs it until one exists.
media.alt: Side-by-side comparison: on the left, a default-deny gate runs known-good payroll software and denies unknown ransomware with no signature needed; on the right, a default-allow gate runs both until the ransomware is recognized as bad.

media.title: Ringfencing: four leashes on an allowed application
media.caption: Word stays approved, but it cannot spawn PowerShell, read the credential store, or reach the internet — while opening its document is allowed.
media.alt: An approved Word application inside a dashed containment ring: arrows show PowerShell launch denied, credential-store registry access denied, external network denied, and document file access allowed.

media.title: The Zero Trust endpoint stack
media.caption: Five deny-by-default layers — Allowlisting, Ringfencing, Elevation, Storage, Network — watched by Web Control, the Testing Environment, Unified Audit, and the Cyber Hero MDR team.
media.alt: A vertical stack of five layers from Allowlisting at the foundation up through Ringfencing, Elevation Control, Storage Control, and Network Control, with side boxes for Web Control, Testing Environment, Unified Audit, and Cyber Hero MDR.

media.title: Application-request triage flow
media.caption: Gather evidence first, then branch: trusted gets a scoped rule, unknown goes to the sandbox, malicious gets a documented deny.
media.alt: Flowchart from request arrival through evidence gathering to a decision diamond branching into three outcomes: approve with a scoped rule, detonate in the Testing Environment then ringfence, or deny with documented evidence.
Diagram of four labeled nodes (user, host, file, domain, IP) joined by labeled directed edges such as logged into, downloaded, and resolved to, illustrating graph vocabulary.
media.caption: Nodes are the things; edges are the relationships. Attackers move along the edges.
media.title: Graph vocabulary: nodes and edges

media.alt: Attack graph with four nodes in a chain: external attacker to VPN gateway to file server to customer database, with a dead-end branch to a printer, showing the shortest path to the crown jewel.
media.caption: The shortest path to the crown jewel is length 3. Break the choke point and the campaign dies.
media.title: Attack graph: shortest path to the crown jewels

media.alt: Seven kill-chain stages as connected graph nodes: reconnaissance, weaponization, delivery, exploitation, installation, command and control, actions. Three alerts are annotated at delivery, installation, and command and control.
media.caption: Three 'unrelated' alerts, one kill-chain subgraph. Correlate by shared entities, not by severity.
media.title: Kill chain as a graph

media.alt: A policy engine at the center of a small graph evaluates an access request from a finance user on an untrusted laptop to an R and D code server. The request is denied because there is no prior relationship edge and the device is untrusted.
media.caption: Valid credentials are not enough. The graph checks device trust, history, and relationships on every request.
media.title: Zero Trust runs on relationships
ML detection pipeline: telemetry to triage
media.caption: How raw telemetry becomes scored alerts: features feed the model, the model scores, analysts triage top-down — and analyst verdicts feed retraining.
media.alt: Flow diagram: telemetry sources feed feature extraction, which feeds an ML model, which outputs scored alerts into an analyst triage queue, with a feedback arrow for retraining.

media.title: UEBA: baseline vs deviation
media.caption: UEBA learns each user's normal hours, locations, and volumes, then scores deviations from that baseline.
media.alt: 24-hour timeline showing a shaded normal login window from 8 AM to 6 PM with normal logins inside it, and a red anomaly marker at 2:47 AM for a foreign login scoring 97 out of 100.

media.title: Indirect prompt injection attack flow
media.caption: An attacker hides instructions in data the agent retrieves; the agent mistakes data for instructions and misuses its tools.
media.alt: Attack flow diagram: hidden instruction in an email is read by an AI agent, which mistakes it for a command and calls a privileged tool, causing fraud; three defense boxes below: sanitize content, least-privilege tools, human approval.
